description: Solo entry by Afraim, a Medical Biotechnology student skilled in computational biology, data analysis, and scientific web UI. Building BASELINE, a personal-baseline-first health self-assessment tool helping astronauts monitor vital indicators across NASA's five spaceflight hazards using verified NASA HRP resources. Closed solo team (not recruiting additional members), though feedback from peers interested in space medicine and human factors is welcome.
summary: BASELINE is a browser-based prototype that helps astronauts assess their own health. It compares six self-measured indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, mood) with each person’s own baseline, shows a neutral state for missing, stale or non-comparable readings, and links indicators to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards through a Hazard Lens. Guidance text is displayed only after the author manually verified it against a cited source. Readings are simulated, thresholds are illustrative, and it is not medical advice. Treatment and escalation guidance is left empty rather than invented.
details:
I built BASELINE as a browser-based health-monitoring prototype for NASA Space Apps 2026. It demonstrates monitoring six indicators: blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood. Its guiding principle is personal baseline first: deviation is not diagnosis. I wanted the person's starting point to remain visible instead of letting general reference ranges dominate. Green, Amber, and Red show configured deviations from fixed, illustrative personal baselines, not diagnoses or medical urgency. This keeps attention on change over time while preserving context for discussion, rather than suggesting that generic ranges define everyone.

Each card shows the latest reading, unit, timestamp, baseline, absolute or percentage change, and a seven-day trend. Expandable tables reveal the readings behind the charts. I added synthetic measurement entry, Test deviation, and Reset demo controls. Heart rate comparisons require resting context; glucose comparisons require fasting context. Other-context readings are logged but remain neutral and not comparable.

I deliberately keep missing data visible. Readings older than 48 hours, missing readings, and absent baselines never default to Green. Entry guards reject malformed values and future timestamps; these are typo checks, not clinical thresholds. Personal baselines remain fixed rather than automatically adapting to new readings.

The Hazard Lens organizes NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. Selecting a hazard highlights associations supplied by eligible claims, with primary, secondary, or operational classifications. I distinguish source statements from interface interpretations and show shared, hazard-wide explanations separately. Neither hazard selection nor body navigation changes deviation calculations. The radiation view explicitly states that the six indicators do not measure radiation exposure.

I made evidence inspectable through the Sources and verification panel. It calculates total claims, verified and unverified counts, and registered sources from local files. Displayed claims include source links and passage locators; interpretation notes remain visible. Drafts and claims failing metadata checks do not populate public guidance. The counts reflect recorded verification flags, not independent scientific certification. NASA and Canadian Space Agency references provide explanatory context, not imported clinical thresholds.

An interactive inline SVG body schematic groups cards for navigation, not anatomical claims. I included equivalent keyboard controls, visible focus states, text labels alongside colors, and accessible chart tables. The responsive layout supports desktop and mobile exploration. Together, these features help users inspect changes, context, and evidence rather than trust unexplained status colors.

I used plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, native SVG, and browser localStorage for synthetic demo history. GitHub Pages provides static hosting with no backend, server database, login, or live device connection. No external libraries or build step are required. The downloaded application also opens directly through index.html without installation or internet access. I used AI assistance through Kilo for code and documentation, and disclose AI-generated artwork. The software needs only an ordinary computer or phone with a modern browser, not specialized medical hardware.

I included 245 offline tests in tests.html. They exercise deviation boundaries, both blood-pressure channels, missing and stale data, context and unit mismatches, entry validation, and tolerance bands. Results appear in a browser pass/fail table without a testing framework. These tests assess implemented software behavior, not medical accuracy or scientific validity.

BASELINE is a transparent demonstration, not a clinically validated or flight-ready monitoring system. All readings, baselines, and thresholds are synthetic. I keep PROTOTYPE and SIMULATED DATA warnings visible during use. It cannot diagnose illness, prescribe treatment, establish radiation exposure, or replace qualified medical judgment. localStorage is not a secure medical record, and users must not enter real personal health data. Scientific review, clinical validation, security safeguards, and operational testing are required before real use.
